signal.title: fix(agent): contain hung sequential tool execution
signal.text: ## Summary Fixes #84719. A lone tool call currently enters `execute_tool_calls_sequential()` without an external deadline. If its handler, transport, middleware, or observer never returns, the conversation thread remains blocked until the Hermes process is restarted. This change adds a per-call sequential supervisor that recovers the turn while preserving existing middleware, approval, persistence, and hook contracts. It is an independent, more defensive alternative to #84795: it also contains late side effects, `/stop`, human waits, stuck observers, worker growth, and cross-round ordering rather than continuing blindly after abandoning a thread. This is a reliability/availability correction with side-effect containment. It is not presented as a security vulnerability. ## Type of change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking reliability correction) - [x] Tests - [x] Documentation ## Root cause - Single-call batches are routed to the sequential executor. - The concurrent executor has an external deadline; the sequential executor called the middleware/handler directly on the conversation thread. - Internal tool timeouts are insufficient when a transport, plugin, or handler stops returning entirely. - Python cannot safely kill an arbitrary running thread, so simply timing out a future can leave late mutations and hooks behind. ## Why this is separate from #84795 #84795 correctly adds a bounded waiter and suppresses late success events, but it deliberately continues later calls after a timed-out worker whose effect is unknown and exempts `clarify` from the deadline after dispatch. This implementation takes a stricter containment approach: - later calls are cancelled when an abandoned worker may still produce an unknown effect; - effectful workers quarantine later mutations across model rounds until they exit; - human-response time is measured and excluded, while post-response processing remains supervised; - observer hooks and abandoned-worker growth are independently bounded; - timeout and capacity controls are user-facing `config.yaml` settings with validation and documentation. The additional surface is intentional: recovery should not let a late worker contradict the canonical result, reorder side effects, or replace one indefinite wait with unbounded detached threads. ## Implementation - Run the complete sequential middleware/dispatch path in a daemon worker under a configurable wall-clock deadline. - Keep human approval time out of the deadline using the existing source-tracked approval gate. - Suspend `clarify` / `setup_mcp` only while their actual handler is waiting, measure that interval explicitly, and extend the effective deadline so it cannot be charged retroactively during post-handler processing. - Make `/stop` wake the owner immediately and propagate cooperative interruption to the worker. - Fence dispatch if timeout wins before execution starts. - Persist a paired synthetic `tool` result with `error_type=tool_timeout` and `effect_disposition=unknown` after a dispatched timeout. - Skip later calls in the same batch after an unknown late effect. - Quarantine later effectful calls across model rounds while an effectful abandoned worker remains alive; read-only diagnostics can continue. - Atomically reserve abandoned-worker capacity before submission, release it on ordinary completion or submit failure, and retain it only while a timed-out worker remains alive. This makes the per-agent cap effective under concurrent entry. - Bound `post_tool_call` observer execution and allow only one detached observer per agent, so a stuck hook cannot re-wedge the owner or leak an unbounded number of threads. - Use ContextVars to preserve normal fast-hook ordering while ensuring a late success observer cannot defeat the canonical timeout result. - Preserve synthetic metadata before persistence/subdirectory-hint transformations. - Reject non-finite timeout and worker-cap configuration values, including YAML-native `.inf`. ## Configuration ```yaml agent: sequential_tool_timeout: 420 max_abandoned_tool_workers: 2 ``` `sequential_tool_timeout: 0` retains the legacy unlimited behavior. Both settings are documented in the configuration guide. ## Regression coverage The new behavior tests cover: - hung single-call recovery and tool-call pairing; - `/stop` responsiveness; - `clarify` and `setup_mcp` human waits; - approval-wait exclusion; - pre-dispatch abandonment fencing; - one canonical terminal hook with late worker completion; - stuck synthetic and success hooks; - subdirectory hints preserving timeout metadata; - same-batch and segmented-batch cancellation; - abandoned-worker capacity; - atomic worker-cap admission under concurrent owners; - cross-round effect quarantine, including homogeneous parallel batches; - ContextVar propagation; - non-finite timeout and worker-cap configuration fallback; - post-handler work after a long human response does not incur the response time retroactively. Verified locally on Windows: - `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/run_agent/test_sequential_tool_deadline.py tests/test_model_tools.py tests/run_agent/test_tool_call_incremental_persistence.py` — 57 passed - `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/run_agent/test_run_agent.py` — 244 passed - `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/run_agent/test_interrupt_propagation.py tests/run_agent/test_concurrent_interrupt.py` — 12 passed - Three additional no-retry stability runs of `test_sequential_tool_deadline.py` — 20/20 passed each run - Ruff on every changed Python file — passed - `git diff --check` — passed An independent final read-only review of the complete 7-file diff returned **PASS with no concrete P0/P1/P2 findings**. It separately exercised human-deadline accounting, atomic worker admission/release, ContextVar reset, hook ownership, and non-finite configuration handling (38 focused tests plus in-memory probes). Two unrelated host-dependent tests remain locally red and reproduce on `origin/main`: a Windows symlink privilege test (`WinError 1314`) and a POSIX-path assertion in the guardrail test. They are not changed or masked here. ## Performance The supervisor deliberately uses per-call daemon workers so one abandoned call cannot starve a shared pool. A local 100-call micro-probe measured approximately 5 ms of supervisory overhead per sequential call. No observer thread is created when no `post_tool_call` hook is registered. ## Files changed - `agent/tool_executor.py` — sequential supervision, effect containment, bounded observer dispatch, atomic worker admission. - `agent/agent_init.py` — validated timeout/cap configuration and per-agent supervisor state. - `model_tools.py` — context-local terminal-hook ownership and handler-completion signaling. - `run_agent.py` — route sequential execution through the supervised path and preserve timeout metadata. - `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` — user-facing defaults. - `website/docs/user-guide/configuration.md` — configuration semantics and operational caveats. - `tests/run_agent/test_sequential_tool_deadline.py` — end-to-end and deterministic concurrency regressions. ## Checklist - [x] Read the contributing guide. - [x] Conventional commit message. - [x] Searched open and closed issues/PRs; the overlap and stricter scope relative to #84795 are documented above. - [x] Diff is limited to the reported root cause and its containment/configuration contracts. - [x] Added regression coverage and ran the repository's canonical test wrapper on the affected suites. - [x] Tested on Windows 11. - [x] Updated user-facing configuration documentation. - [x] Considered cross-platform behavior; the implementation uses portable `threading`, `contextvars`, and `concurrent.futures` primitives. - [x] Tool schemas are unchanged (N/A).

signal.title: fix(gateway): anchor fallback secret patterns with ASCII word lookarounds
signal.text: Fixes #81073 ## Problem `_GATEWAY_SECRET_PATTERNS` in `gateway/run.py` anchored every credential pattern with `\b`. Under Python 3's default Unicode semantics, a CJK or fullwidth letter is a `\w` character, so a credential glued directly to one (`xx中sk-...`, `xx１sk-...`) is **not** at a `\b` boundary. On the fallback-only path the token was left unredacted: ```python PAT = re.compile(r"\bsk-[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_\-]{12,}\b") assert PAT.search("xx " + TOKEN) # ASCII neighbor → matches assert PAT.search("xx中" + TOKEN) is None # CJK-glued → no match ``` ## Fix Replace the `\b` anchors with ASCII word lookarounds `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` / `(?![A-Za-z0-9_])` across all seven patterns. Behavior: - ASCII-neighbored tokens still redact exactly as before (no regression). - CJK- and fullwidth-glued tokens now redact too. - A token embedded inside an ASCII identifier (`xxsk-...yy`) is still not matched — same boundary semantics as `\b`. - The `Bearer` pattern still preserves its prefix via `group(1)`. ## Tests New `tests/gateway/test_gateway_secret_patterns_cjk.py` parametrizes all seven token shapes across: - CJK-glued redaction (the reported regression) - fullwidth-digit-glued redaction - ASCII-neighbor redaction (no regression) - embedded-in-ASCII-word non-matching (no over-match) - Bearer prefix preservation - prose-without-tokens unchanged 30 new tests pass; `tests/gateway/test_telegram_noise_filter.py` (133 tests) still passes.

signal.title: fix(file-safety): whitelist kernel sinks (/dev/null etc.) in write-safe-root guard
signal.text: ## Summary Fixes a false-positive denial in the `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT` guard: writes to kernel character-device sinks like `/dev/null` were being rejected as "outside HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT" even though those paths are OS-level no-ops used routinely for legitimate shell redirection. **Reproducer** (on `main` before this change, in any container with `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/opt/data`): ``` $ hermes chat -q 'run: echo x > /dev/null' Write denied: '/dev/null' is outside HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT (/opt/data). ... ``` `/dev/null` and its siblings cannot be made to persist state, so gating them behind the safe-root check only breaks legitimate patterns (silencing chatter, discarding stderr, ...) with no safety benefit. ## Fix Additive-only, 45 lines in `agent/file_safety.py`: - A five-entry `_KERNEL_SINK_ALLOWLIST` frozenset: `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, `/dev/tty`, `/dev/zero`. - A helper `_is_kernel_sink()` that normalizes with `os.path.normpath` + `os.path.abspath` (deliberately **not** `realpath`) and membership-tests against the set. - `_classify_write_denial()` gains one short-circuit at the top: `if _is_kernel_sink(path): return None`. Everything else in the guard (credential denylist, hermes-internal path checks, safe-root containment) is untouched. ### Why `abspath` and not `realpath` If we resolved symlinks, a symlink at e.g. `/opt/data/evil -> /dev/null` would inherit the allowlist and let an arbitrary out-of-tree name bypass the safe-root check. Using `abspath` on the user-supplied string means **only literal** `/dev/null` etc. short-circuit; a symlink pointing at one still gets rejected on its own absolute path. There is an explicit test for this attack shape (`test_symlink_to_dev_null_not_bypassed`). ## Tests 11 new cases appended to `tests/agent/test_file_safety.py` under a new `TestKernelSinkAllowlist` class: - Parametrized sweep — every one of the five sinks is allowed under a mismatched `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/tmp/safe` - `/dev/random` (not on allowlist) still returns `'safe_root'` - `/etc/passwd`-style credential paths still return `'credential'` - Genuinely out-of-tree paths still return `'safe_root'` - Symlink-bypass regression — `/tmp/evil -> /dev/null` gets rejected on its own abspath - Helper recognizes normalized variants like `/dev/./null` - Helper handles empty/bogus input without raising ## Invariants preserved - Public API unchanged (no signature or return-type changes on `_classify_write_denial`) - Error message shape for genuine rejections unchanged (still `outside HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT (...)`) - No new config keys, env vars, or user-facing surface - No changes to credential denylist, hermes-internal path checks, or safe-root containment logic - Behavior is defined by the frozenset — no user-configurable extra entries (explicitly out of scope per the original request) ## Out of scope - User-configurable extra allowlist entries - Any redesign of the `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT` mechanism itself
signal.author: jrdowson

signal.title: Custom providers not shared across profiles + no reliable add path in Desktop/CLI
signal.text: ## Summary Adding a custom provider is painful and inconsistent across profiles and surfaces. Three related problems: ### 1. Custom providers are not propagated to other profiles When I add a custom provider in one profile (e.g. `default`), it does **not** appear in my other profiles (`coding-agent`, `telegram`). There is no "apply to all profiles" option. To use the same custom provider everywhere I have to manually copy the `providers:` / `custom_providers:` block and the API key into every profile's `config.yaml` and `.env` by hand. This is error-prone (I ended up with mismatched provider names between profiles) and defeats the purpose of having isolated-but-shareable profiles. Expected: a custom provider added once should be selectable in every profile, or there should be a clear "copy provider to profile X" / "apply to all profiles" action. ### 2. No working way to add a custom provider from Desktop app or CLI - **Desktop app:** the "add custom provider" UI hangs / appears to succeed but then reports the provider is "already added" even when it is not present in the active profile's config. The provider never actually shows up in the model/provider picker. - **CLI:** `hermes config set` cannot be trusted for nested keys — it appends a duplicate top-level block instead of editing the existing key (tracked separately in #71047, still open). So there is no reliable CLI path to add a custom provider to a non-default profile either. Expected: a documented, working flow (`hermes model` picker, `hermes config`, or Desktop settings) to register a custom provider for the *currently active* profile. ### 3. Profile switching itself has open issues Related: #85777 (local profile switch reuses default socket after update) and #71047 (config set duplicates top-level key). Both make the multi-profile experience fragile, which amplifies problem #1. ## Environment - Hermes Agent: current `main` (pyproject ~0.20.x) - Platform: Windows 10 - Profiles: `default`, `coding-agent`, `telegram` - Custom providers involved: `9router` (local OpenAI-compatible endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:20128/v1`) and `AgentRouter` (`https://agentrouter.org/v1`) ## What I did (manual reproduction of the gap) 1. Registered `9router` + `AgentRouter` in `default` via Desktop app → worked there. 2. Switched to `coding-agent` / `telegram` → neither provider appeared in the picker. 3. Tried adding them again in the Desktop app for the active profile → UI hung / said "already added", nothing written to `config.yaml`. 4. Had to copy `providers:` and `custom_providers:` blocks + `.env` keys manually into each profile's files. ## Suggested improvement - Custom providers should be stored at a shared layer (or have an explicit "share with profile…" control) so they don't have to be re-added per profile. - Fix/provide a reliable add-custom-provider path in both the Desktop app and `hermes model` / `hermes config` (the Desktop "already added" hang and the `config set` duplicate-key bug must be resolved first).

signal.title: fix(agent): redact secrets from persisted verification-evidence commands
signal.text: ## What changed `classify_verification_command()` stores the raw terminal command verbatim in `verification_evidence.db`. `verification_status()` later returns that field unredacted, and the gateway's `verification.status` RPC (`tui_gateway/methods_session.py`) replays it to the TUI/desktop client as-is. A verification command that embeds a credential inline (e.g. an ad-hoc `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ..."` check, or an env-var-prefixed test invocation) persists that secret to disk and re-surfaces it over the RPC wire. The same code path already redacts the command's *output* via `redact_terminal_output()` before it reaches this module — see `tools/terminal_tool.py`'s spill-file and in-memory `output` handling — but never redacted the command line itself. ## Fix Force-redact `command` at the single `VerificationEvidence` construction site in `classify_verification_command()` (the sole writer chokepoint — `record_terminal_result()` has one caller, `tools/terminal_tool.py`). Uses `redact_sensitive_text(command, force=True)`, mirroring `redact_terminal_output`'s `force=True` posture for safety boundaries that must never emit raw credentials regardless of the user's `security.redact_secrets` preference. Matching/classification logic still runs against the original command — only the persisted/returned field is redacted. ## Testing - Two new regression tests: one on the in-memory `classify_verification_command()` result, one on the full `record_terminal_result()` -> `verification_status()` round trip (the actual RPC-exposed path, checked via `json.dumps(status)` and a direct read of the `verification_events` table). - Mutation-verified: both fail against the pre-fix code (`command=command` instead of `command=redact_sensitive_text(command, force=True)`). - `tests/agent/test_verification_evidence.py`, `tests/agent/test_verification_evidence_fd_leak.py`, `tests/agent/test_redact.py`, `tests/tools/test_process_registry.py`, `tests/tools/test_terminal_tool.py`, `tests/tools/test_terminal_tool_requirements.py`, `tests/tools/test_terminal_tool_pty_fallback.py` — 188 tests, all green. - `ruff check` clean. ## Note on adjacent PR #62736 Open PR #62736 (`fix/62728-verify-inference`) also touches `agent/verification_evidence.py`, adding a shape/outcome inference layer to the same `classify_verification_command()` function. It does not modify the `command=` line this PR changes (only the `kind=` line a few lines below) — textual proximity, not a semantic conflict. ## Checklist - [x] Regression tests added, mutation-verified against pre-fix code - [x] Broad neighbor test suite green (188 tests) - [x] `ruff check` clean - [x] Fresh competitor search performed before opening

signal.title: fix(tool-search): keep MCP bridge cache-stable
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Fixes Tool Search's stale embedded catalog while keeping ordinary MCP catalog changes and context compression prompt-cache stable. The three bridge schemas (`tool_search`, `tool_describe`, and `tool_call`) are fixed and remain present whenever Tool Search is enabled, including when the live deferred catalog is empty. Bridge calls resolve the current session-scoped registry at invocation time, so MCP additions, removals, equal-count swaps, and schema edits no longer mutate the model-facing `tools=` prefix. The model receives discovery context through an API-only catalog snapshot attached to a real user turn. String user content stays clean while the exact API sidecar is persisted for byte-identical replay. When the catalog changes, Hermes attaches a superseding snapshot to the next real user turn instead of rebuilding bridge schemas or inserting a synthetic user-role message. Slow MCP startup is handled without waiting for every server. A snapshot lists tools currently ready plus the names of in-scope MCP servers still initializing. Pending-server state participates in the fingerprint, so a later real user turn carries a superseding snapshot when those servers become ready or fail. Snapshot construction does not import the MCP stack merely to inspect status. Compression also preserves discovery continuity. A turn may decide that an older snapshot is already present and then compress that older user row before its next model call. Before committing a successful compression boundary, Hermes re-anchors the current snapshot onto the newest surviving real user message's `api_content` (or a multimodal text part). If no genuine user row survives, it reuses an existing compression user scaffold rather than creating another message. Repeated compression checks for the exact current snapshot, so it is sent after every boundary without stacking duplicate copies in one message. ## Why Embedding the deferred-tool count and catalog inside bridge descriptions made every toolset edit change `tools=`, invalidating the cached conversation prefix. Moving discovery metadata out of the bridge solves that, but two additional boundaries matter: - waiting for all MCP servers would move potentially long startup latency onto the chat critical path; - compression can remove the catalog-bearing historical turn and continue calling the model in the same turn, before the normal next-turn re-announcement runs. This PR separates those concerns: - stable bridge schemas preserve the cached prefix; - append-only metadata on real user turns preserves role alternation; - pending server names keep not-yet-ready capability domains discoverable; - live registry lookup makes newly registered tools usable immediately; - compression re-anchors the current snapshot before persistence and retry; - resumed sessions compare the live schema/pending fingerprint with persisted `api_content`, reusing an identical snapshot or superseding a stale one. This PR does not change surface-specific MCP startup scheduling. It makes Tool Search catalog construction and replay safe when discovery is incomplete or conversation history is compressed. ## Related Issue Fixes #72560 ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [x] 📝 Documentation update - [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - Replaced dynamic bridge counts/listings with byte-stable schemas and live registry discovery. - Kept the bridge present across the zero-tool boundary. - Moved compact catalog snapshots onto the API copy of real user turns. - Fingerprinted complete scoped schemas, rendered manifest form, and pending MCP server names. - Added a non-blocking pending-server probe that never imports `tools.mcp_tool` solely for snapshot generation. - Published a superseding snapshot on the next real user turn when a pending server becomes ready or fails. - Re-anchored the current snapshot at every successful compression boundary before in-place or rotation persistence. - Preserved existing plugin/memory sidecar content, handled multimodal turns, and deduplicated repeated compression anchors. - Covered zero-human-turn compression by reusing an existing user scaffold without changing role alternation. - Kept direct-schema mode schema-sensitive while preserving the exact `agent.tools` object in stable-bridge mode. - Updated Tool Search documentation and regression coverage. ## How to Test 1. Start a session with Tool Search enabled while an MCP server is connecting. 2. Verify the first real user turn lists ready tools and pending server names without changing bridge schemas. 3. Let the server connect; verify `tool_search` sees the live tools and the next real user turn carries a superseding snapshot. 4. Compress a later turn after the original snapshot-bearing user row has entered the compressible region. 5. Verify the compressed request and persisted transcript contain exactly one current snapshot on the newest surviving user message. 6. Repeat in both in-place and rotation compression modes, then resume the session and verify byte-identical `api_content` replay. 7. Set `tools.tool_search.enabled: off`; verify direct tool definitions continue to rebuild normally. Validated on the pushed commit: ```shell scripts/run_tests.sh -j 2 \ tests/agent/test_turn_context.py \ tests/run_agent/test_compression_persistence.py -q # 36 passed scripts/run_tests.sh -j 6 \ tests/tools/test_tool_search.py \ tests/tools/test_refresh_agent_mcp_tools.py \ tests/agent/test_turn_context.py \ tests/agent/test_api_content_sidecar.py \ tests/run_agent/test_compression_persistence.py \ tests/agent/test_compression_rotation_state.py \ tests/agent/test_compression_concurrent_fork.py \ tests/agent/test_context_compressor_zero_user_provenance.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins.py \ tests/cli/test_cli_mcp_config_watch.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_mcp_reload_confirm_gate.py \ tests/gateway/test_mcp_reload_refreshes_cached_agents.py \ tests/tui_gateway/test_mcp_reload_rev.py \ tests/test_tui_mcp_late_refresh.py \ tests/tui_gateway/test_mcp_late_refresh_thread_owner.py -q # 215 passed # Under a heavily loaded run, the existing concurrent-compression lock test # exceeded its 10s timing window once and passed on the runner retry. scripts/run_tests.sh -j 1 tests/agent/test_compression_concurrent_fork.py -q # 16 passed cleanly in isolation .venv/bin/ruff check \ agent/conversation_compression.py \ tests/agent/test_turn_context.py \ tests/run_agent/test_compression_persistence.py # All checks passed git diff --check # clean ``` ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) - [x] I searched for existing PRs to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains only changes related to this fix - [ ] I've run the complete `pytest tests/ -q` suite; the targeted cross-entry regression suites above pass - [x] I've added tests for the changed behavior - [x] I've tested on macOS 27.0, Python 3.13 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] Relevant documentation is updated - [x] `cli-config.yaml.example` update — N/A (no config keys changed) - [x] `CONTRIBUTING.md` / `AGENTS.md` update — N/A - [x] Cross-platform impact considered; implementation uses platform-independent message/config/registry state - [x] Bridge descriptions remain intentionally byte-stable

signal.title: fix(config): guard security-policy keys in hermes config set/unset
signal.text: Fixes #81101 ## Problem `set_config_value()` / `unset_config_value()` accepted ANY key, including security-policy keys (`approvals.*`, `security.*`, `command_allowlist`). An agent could run `hermes config set approvals.mode off` to disable the approval gate mid-session with no operator confirmation — the config cache is mtime-keyed, so the write takes effect immediately. The file tools already hard-deny agent writes to `config.yaml` (`tools/file_tools.py`), so the sanctioned CLI was a one-command bypass of the exact protection the file-tool deny exists to provide. ## Fix 1. **`hermes_cli/config.py`** — `set_config_value()` now refuses security-policy keys unless `--force` is passed (the explicit operator override typed at the CLI). `unset_config_value()` refuses them outright (no `--force` on that subcommand). A clear message points to `hermes approvals` or `--force`/direct edit. 2. **`hermes_cli/approval_mode.py`** — the canonical operator path (`hermes approvals` / `/approvals`) passes `force=True`, so it keeps working (it's the sanctioned way to change `approvals.mode`). 3. **`tools/approval.py`** — new `DANGEROUS_PATTERNS` entry so the terminal approval gate flags `hermes config set (approvals|security|command_allowlist)` — including the `--force` variant — the same way `sed`/`tee` on `config.yaml` are gated. ## Tests - `tests/hermes_cli/test_set_config_value.py::TestSensitiveConfigKeyGuard` — refusal without force (parametrized over `approvals.*`/`security.*`/`command_allowlist`), allow with force, unset refusal, benign keys unaffected, refusal fires before YAML parse, `approvals.mode` message points to `hermes approvals`. - `tests/tools/test_approval.py::TestConfigSetSecurityPolicy` — dangerous detection (incl. `--force` and `-p <profile>` variants) + benign `config set` not flagged. 101 targeted tests pass. (Two unrelated pre-existing failures in `tests/tools/test_approval.py` are Windows-only symlink/rm-tmp issues, confirmed failing on the base commit.)
signal.author: Enough1122

signal.title: perf(stt): configurable beam_size and startup prewarm for local whisper
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Two independent sources of fixed latency on every local-STT turn. Neither changes behaviour for existing callers. ### beam_size was hardcoded to 5 `build_local_transcribe_kwargs` is the single owner of every local faster-whisper call, and it pinned faster-whisper's accuracy-oriented default on all of them — including interactive voice. Beam search is the dominant decode cost on short utterances, where a wider beam buys very little over greedy. Now `stt.local.beam_size`, **defaulting to 5** so batch jobs and `hermes transcribe` are unaffected; realtime users opt into 1. ### The model loaded lazily on first use `_transcribe_local` builds the model under `_local_model_lock`, so the first turn after every restart paid the load on top of its own decode — the turn a user is most likely to judge responsiveness on. Warm it on a daemon thread during lifespan startup, beside the existing `_warm_gateway_module()`. It is a no-op unless local STT is the configured provider, so a cloud-STT backend never pulls a multi-hundred-MB model into memory, and every failure is swallowed: the lazy path in `_transcribe_local` remains the source of truth. ## Type of Change - [x] ♻️ Performance (no behaviour change at default config) ## Changes Made - `tools/transcription_tools.py` — `_BEAM_SIZE_DEFAULT = 5`; read/validate `stt.local.beam_size` - `hermes_cli/web_server.py` — `_warm_local_stt_model()` on a daemon thread at startup - `tests/tools/test_stt_beam_size.py` — new ## Measurements Mac mini M4, `small`, int8, CPU: | | beam 5 | beam 1 | |---|---|---| | 7.2s utterance | 1.68s | **1.14s** (identical output) | | 5.0s utterance | 1.97s | **1.74s** | The gain is utterance-dependent — larger on the longer clip — so this is a knob rather than a default flip. Prewarm, from the startup log: ``` INFO hermes_cli.web_server: STT prewarm: faster-whisper 'small' ready in 1.68s ``` That 1.68s previously landed on the user's first spoken turn. ## How to test ```bash pytest tests/tools/test_stt_beam_size.py -v ``` For the prewarm, set `stt.provider: local` and start the dashboard — the log line above appears during startup, and the first transcription no longer stalls. Set `stt.provider` to any cloud backend and confirm the line is absent and no model is loaded. ## What platforms Tested on macOS 15.5 (Apple Silicon). The beam_size change is pure config plumbing. The prewarm is a `threading.Thread` with no platform-specific code, but note it inherits `_transcribe_local`'s existing Apple-Silicon CPU/int8 device selection, so the measured load times will differ elsewhere.

signal.title: [Bug] Hermes Desktop (Linux/Wayland): image paste fails — clipboard image offered as application/octet-stream not recognized
signal.text: ## Bug Description Pasting a screenshot/image into the **Hermes desktop app** fails on a COSMIC/Wayland Linux desktop in every paste method (Ctrl+V, right-click paste, "paste image"), even though the system clipboard correctly holds the image and attaching the same image via the file picker / drag-and-drop works fine. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Press PrtScn (or capture with the COSMIC screenshot tool) to copy a screenshot. 2. Open the Hermes desktop app chat box. 3. Try to attach the image by pasting: Ctrl+V, right-click > paste, or the "+ / paste image" action. 4. Observe: a toast "No image found in clipboard" appears and the image does not attach. 5. As a control: attach the *same* image via the + file picker or drag-and-drop — it attaches correctly. ## Expected Behavior Copying an image (screenshot) to the system clipboard and pasting it into the Hermes desktop chat should attach the image, matching every other modern desktop app. ## Actual Behavior Image pasting fails with "No image found in clipboard"; only manual file attach works. ## Investigation / Root Cause Evidence - System clipboard holds the image fine: `wl-paste --list-types` shows the payload is offered as `application/octet-stream` (not `image/png`), and `wl-paste | od` returns valid PNG magic bytes (`89 50 4e 47`). - Hermes desktop's image-paste path is Electron `clipboard.readImage()` inside the IPC handler `hermes:saveClipboardImage` (`electron/main.ts`). Electron's `readImage()` only recognizes items advertised as `image/png`; an `octet-stream`-offered image returns empty, producing the `noClipboardImage` toast. - A patch adding a `wl-paste --type image/png` (and plain `wl-paste` + PNG-magic) fallback to that handler was built, deployed, and tested on the running app — it did NOT fix paste. This indicates the failure is not isolated to the clipboard-read layer but sits between the renderer paste event and the Electron main-process handler (the renderer's Ctrl+V paste path likely never invokes `saveClipboardImage` for an image-only clipboard). The patch was reverted. - The desktop app does not implement the `/paste` command (that is a CLI/TUI feature), so the documented reliable image-paste path is unavailable on desktop. ## Environment - OS: Pop!_OS 24.04 (COSMIC desktop), Wayland session (`XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland`) - Hermes version: 0.20.0 (desktop app) - Electron main: `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts` ## Suggested Direction Investigate the desktop renderer's paste handler (Electron desktop composer) so that a Wayland server offering an image-clipboard item as `application/octet-stream` is still recognized and attached (e.g., a fallback that shells out to `wl-paste` on Linux/Wayland, or broadening the accepted MIME types in `hermes:saveClipboardImage`).

signal.title: Add copilot-cli skill for ACP + print-mode delegation
signal.text: ## Summary Adds `skills/autonomous-ai-agents/copilot-cli/SKILL.md`, a sibling to the existing `claude-code`, `codex`, and `opencode` skills. Closes a documentation gap: Hermes already ships the `copilot-acp` provider entry and the `agent/copilot_acp_client.py` shim, but there was no skill teaching the agent how to delegate work to GitHub Copilot CLI the way it does for the other coding agents. ## What's in the skill Three orchestration modes are documented end-to-end: 1. **ACP delegation (preferred)** — `delegate_task(acp_command="copilot")`, including `acp_args` overrides for `--allow-all-tools`, `--add-dir`, `--model`, `--effort`. 2. **Print mode** — `copilot -p ... --allow-all-tools --silent` for one-shot scripted runs from `terminal()`, with permission-pattern syntax (`shell(git:*)`, `write`, `url(...)`, `<mcp>(<tool>)`). 3. **Interactive TUI** — background + PTY pattern matching the `codex` / `opencode` skills, with the slash-command reference (`/init`, `/plan`, `/diff`, `/pr`, `/review`, `/research`, `/agent`, `/skills`, `/mcp`, `/model`, `/effort`, `/context`, `/share`, etc.). Also covered: - Environment variables (`HERMES_COPILOT_ACP_COMMAND`, `HERMES_COPILOT_ACP_ARGS`, `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL`, `COPILOT_MODEL`, `COPILOT_HOME`, plus the BYOK `COPILOT_PROVIDER_*` set). - Comparison matrix vs `claude-code` / `codex` / `opencode` to help the agent pick the right tool. - Pitfalls: approval-prompt deadlocks under ACP, path-verification gotchas, `/exit` vs Ctrl+C, BYOK quirks, auto-update interruptions. - Rules for Hermes agents: default to ACP delegation, always pass `--allow-all-tools` non-interactively, state cwd in `context`, restrict toolsets, etc. ## Why a skill, not a tool Per CONTRIBUTING.md, Copilot CLI integration is best expressed as instructions + existing tool calls (`delegate_task`, `terminal`, `process`). No new Python code is required because the ACP client shim already exists in the repo. ## Verification - Cross-checked the SKILL.md flag/env-var reference against `copilot --help`, `copilot help permissions`, and `copilot help environment` from `@github/copilot` (current release at the time of writing). - Verified the ACP transport path matches `agent/copilot_acp_client.py` (binary resolution + default args `['--acp', '--stdio']`). - Verified `delegate_task` honours `acp_command` / `acp_args` overrides via `tools/delegate_tool.py`. ## Files - `skills/autonomous-ai-agents/copilot-cli/SKILL.md` (new, 283 lines)

signal.title: fix(tools): stop browser_cdp frame_id routing from skipping private-page SSRF guard
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? `browser_cdp(..., frame_id=...)` had two private-page / SSRF gaps on the OOPIF path: (1) a non-dict `params` value skipped the clear validation error and could let the guard fail open, and (2) even with valid params, the guard only checked the top-level page URL before supervisor dispatch, so a public parent could embed a private OOPIF and still receive page-content CDP such as `Runtime.evaluate`. This PR closes both paths with shared fail-closed checks before child-session dispatch. ### Symptom A `browser_cdp` call that sets `frame_id` and passes a truthy non-dict `params` (for example a string) does not return `'params' must be an object/dict`. Separately, when the top-level page is public but the selected OOPIF URL/origin is private (or still empty), page-content CDP can still reach the child session. ### Impact Malformed `params` on the `frame_id` path can silently skip the private-page / SSRF boundary that other `browser_cdp` entry points enforce after validating `params`. A public top-level page with a private child OOPIF can also expose private frame content through `frame_id` routing. Blast radius beyond these paths was not measured. ### Bug Cause **Trigger:** `tools/browser_cdp_tool.py` `browser_cdp()` / `_browser_cdp_via_supervisor()` - `frame_id` early-return before `isinstance(params, dict)`; private-page guard uses top-level `_current_page_private_url` only; selected-frame metadata is available but was not checked before child-session dispatch. **Causal chain:** 1. Caller passes `frame_id` with either non-dict `params`, or a well-formed call targeting a private OOPIF under a public top page. 2. Non-dict `params` AttributeErrors inside the guard probe; broad except fail-opens. Or the top-page probe returns public while the child frame is private / metadata-empty. 3. Call reaches `_browser_cdp_via_supervisor` and dispatches into the child CDP session without a validation error or frame-level private-page block. **Why it is wrong:** Params validation lived only on the post-early-return / stateless branch, while the guard is intentionally fail-open for probe failures. Frame routing resolves child URL/origin but never validated them before page-content sinks. **Working sibling / contrast:** Without `frame_id`, non-dict `params` already returned a clear validation error. Top-level private pages already blocked restricted methods; the gap is specifically the selected OOPIF address. **Ruled out:** Not a missing private-page guard call on `frame_id` for well-formed top-level-private cases - that path already invoked the top-page guard. The remaining gaps are malformed params + child-frame address coverage. ### Fix Validate `params` as a dict before the `frame_id` early-return. After resolving the selected frame (frame_tree or raw `_frames` fallback), validate URL/origin for private/internal addresses before dispatch; fail closed when an OOPIF has a `session_id` but empty URL/origin metadata. Retain `_CDP_PRIVATE_PAGE_ALLOWED_METHODS` so navigation/inspection still works on blocked frames. ## Related Issue Fixes #80846 ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [x] Security fix ## Changes Made - `tools/browser_cdp_tool.py` - move params dict validation above the `frame_id` early-return; validate selected frame URL/origin (and empty-metadata OOPIF) before supervisor dispatch; keep navigation/inspection allowlist - `tests/tools/test_browser_cdp_tool.py` - regression coverage for non-dict params, public-top/private-child OOPIF, raw `_frames` fallback, allowlist survival, and empty URL/origin fail-closed ## How to Test 1. Manual: with the private-page guard active, call `browser_cdp(method='Runtime.evaluate', params='not-a-dict', frame_id='...')` and confirm the tool returns a params object/dict validation error (not a successful supervisor dispatch). 2. Manual / unit: public top-level page + private OOPIF `frame_id` must block `Runtime.evaluate` / `DOM.getDocument`; allowlisted methods such as `Page.reload` must still dispatch; OOPIF with `session_id` but empty url/origin must block page-content CDP. 3. Automated: ```bash scripts/run_tests.sh tests/tools/test_browser_cdp_tool.py -q ``` ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [x] I've run `scripts/run_tests.sh` on relevant tests and all tests pass - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11 (WSL test runner) ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings) - N/A - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys - N/A - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows - N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility) - N/A (validation helpers are platform-agnostic) - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior - N/A (behavior matches the documented params object contract and private-page boundary on sibling paths)

signal.title: Gateway hits macOS fd limit (256): OSError Too many open files
signal.text: ## Problem On macOS, the default `launchctl limit maxfiles` soft limit is **256**. Hermes gateway processes with multiple profiles + MCP servers routinely exceed this: ``` trade-paper gateway: 286 fds (198 IPv4, 50 REG, 20 PIPE) ``` When the limit is hit, any file operation fails with: ``` OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files: '.sessions_*.tmp' ``` This crashes session saves, kanban dispatches, and any tool that opens files. ## Root cause - Each MCP server subprocess (playwright, sequential-thinking, memory, brave-search) maintains persistent pipes/sockets - Multiple profiles each run their own gateway with independent MCP connections - Hermes never closes idle MCP connections or monitors fd usage - No startup warning when `ulimit -n` is near capacity ## Workaround Manually add `SoftResourceLimits` → `NumberOfFiles: 4096` to each gateway launchd plist. ## Suggested fixes 1. **Startup detection**: Check `resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)` at gateway start, warn if soft limit < 1024 2. **MCP lazy init**: Don't connect all MCP servers at startup — connect on first tool call 3. **Idle MCP timeout**: Close MCP connections idle for N minutes, reconnect on demand 4. **Periodic fd check**: Log warning in gateway loop if fd count exceeds 80% of soft limit ## Environment - macOS 26.5 (Apple Silicon) - Hermes 3 profiles (default, research, trade-paper) - 6 MCP servers configured - Python 3.x, launchd-managed gateways
signal.author: BournYSix

signal.title: fix(desktop): distinguish pooled profile backends
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Fixes local Desktop profile switching after pooled connection descriptors began carrying `profile` for WebSocket URL minting. `sharedPrimaryRoute()` inferred that any descriptor with `profile` was served by the shared primary backend. Local pooled descriptors also carry `profile`, so a named local profile was misclassified and Desktop reused the default socket instead of opening the profile's persistent WebSocket. This change gives the shared-primary route an explicit `sharedPrimary` marker and checks that marker instead of overloading `profile` with two meanings. ## Related Issue Fixes #85777 ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts`: marks only profile-scoped primary descriptors as `sharedPrimary`. - `apps/desktop/src/global.d.ts`: types the explicit route discriminator. - `apps/desktop/src/store/gateway.ts`: distinguishes shared-primary descriptors from profile-owned pooled descriptors. - `apps/desktop/src/store/gateway-shared-remote.test.ts`: covers both sides of the routing invariant, including a pooled descriptor that carries `profile`. ## How to Test 1. Configure Desktop with local `default` and local named profiles. 2. Launch Desktop on `default` and select a named profile from the profile rail. 3. Confirm the named backend receives a persistent WebSocket and the sidebar/agent context switches to it. 4. Switch back to `default` and confirm the primary socket is restored. Automated checks: ```bash cd apps/desktop npm test -- --run src/store/gateway-shared-remote.test.ts src/store/profile.test.ts # 2 files passed, 13 tests passed npm run lint # 0 errors (88 pre-existing warnings) ``` `npm run typecheck` passed on the checkout used to build and validate the installed fix. After rebasing onto current `origin/main` (`edb33be51`), it is presently blocked by an unrelated baseline error in `src/app/chat/hooks/use-composer-actions.test.ts:294`: the new `ComposerActionsScope.update` field is missing from that test fixture. This PR does not modify that code. The rebuilt macOS package was installed locally and the reporter confirmed profile switching works after restart. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass — N/A: Desktop TypeScript-only change; focused Vitest coverage ran instead - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: macOS 26.6.1, Apple silicon ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation — N/A; internal routing bug - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` — N/A; no config change - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` — N/A; no workflow change - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact — the explicit descriptor marker is platform-independent - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas — N/A; no tool change ## Screenshots / Logs Before the fix, the named backend started and its one-shot startup probe connected, but no persistent WebSocket followed: ```text Starting Hermes backend for profile "fiction-writer" HERMES_BACKEND_READY port=64271 Hermes backend listening on 127.0.0.1:64271 ... tui_gateway.ws: ws accepted ... tui_gateway.ws: ws closed ... messages=0 ``` After rebuilding with this change and restarting Desktop, switching between `default` and the local named profile works normally.

signal.title: fix(desktop): local profile switch reuses default socket after update
signal.text: ## Summary After a recent Desktop update, selecting any local named profile from the profile rail can leave Desktop attached to the default profile. The named backend starts successfully, but Desktop never opens its persistent WebSocket and continues using the primary/default socket. This affects current `main` and makes local multi-profile switching appear inert: the profile is selectable, but the sidebar/active agent remains on the same profile. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop on macOS 26.6.1 (Apple silicon) - Local primary profile: `default` - Local named profile: `fiction-writer` - Reproduced from current `main` around `486f4ace20ba75401681c0915ab79a0968fa6bb1` - Confirmed still present after fetching current `origin/main` ## Reproduction 1. Configure Desktop with the local `default` profile and at least one local named profile. 2. Launch Desktop on `default`. 3. Select the named profile from the profile rail. 4. Observe that the named backend starts and passes the one-shot WebSocket probe. 5. Observe that no persistent WebSocket is opened for the named profile and the Desktop context remains attached to the primary/default socket. ## Expected behavior A local named profile should use its own pooled backend and persistent WebSocket. The sidebar, sessions, model, tools, and agent context should move to that profile. ## Actual behavior The local pooled descriptor is mistaken for a shared-primary descriptor. Desktop reuses the primary/default socket instead of dialing the named profile's pooled backend. Representative log sequence: ```text Starting Hermes backend for profile "fiction-writer" ... HERMES_BACKEND_READY port=64271 Hermes backend listening on 127.0.0.1:64271 ... tui_gateway.ws: ws accepted ... tui_gateway.ws: ws closed ... messages=0 ``` The accepted/closed connection is the startup probe. There is no subsequent persistent profile WebSocket. ## Root cause `apps/desktop/src/store/gateway.ts::sharedPrimaryRoute()` currently treats the presence of `connection.profile` as proof that the descriptor uses the shared primary backend: ```ts return Boolean(conn && typeof conn === 'object' && (conn as { profile?: string }).profile) ``` However, `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts::spawnPoolBackend()` intentionally returns `profile` for local pooled descriptors as well. That profile value is needed so fresh WebSocket URL minting targets the correct backend. Therefore both of these descriptors carry `profile`: - a profile scoped onto the shared primary backend; - a dedicated local/remote pooled backend. The discriminator conflates those two routes. `ensureGatewayForProfile()` then takes the shared-primary branch for a local pool profile and never dials its socket. ## Proposed fix Add an explicit `sharedPrimary` marker only when `ensureBackend()` returns a profile-scoped primary descriptor, and make `sharedPrimaryRoute()` check that marker rather than inferring route ownership from `profile`. A regression test should assert both sides of the invariant: - `{ profile, sharedPrimary: true }` activates the primary socket; - a pooled descriptor carrying `{ profile }` still dials its own socket. ## Verification The proposed patch was tested locally: ```text Test Files 2 passed (2) Tests 13 passed (13) ``` Commands: ```bash cd apps/desktop npm test -- --run src/store/gateway-shared-remote.test.ts src/store/profile.test.ts npm run typecheck npm run pack ``` After installing the rebuilt package and restarting Desktop, switching between `default` and the local named profile works normally again.

signal.title: [Bug]: grok-4.6 reasoning effort silently dropped; max/ultra 400 on send path
signal.text: ## Bug Description When using an xAI OAuth account (grok-4.6 / grok-4.5), the reasoning-effort setting is either **silently ignored** or **hard-fails the request with HTTP 400**, depending on the level chosen. Two distinct defects on the send path (not the picker): **A. `grok-4.6` is missing from the `grok_supports_reasoning_effort` allowlist** (`agent/model_metadata.py`, ~line 555). Any effort selected for grok-4.6 is never attached to the request at all — the UI shows a choice that has zero effect. Verified live against `api.x.ai` (`/v1/responses`): grok-4.6 **accepts** `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`. **B. Unsupported levels (`max`, `ultra`) are sent verbatim and fail the whole request** with `400 Invalid reasoning effort`. There is no per-model clamp on the send path — only a hard-coded xAI map in `agent/transports/codex.py` that predates 4.6 (it folds `xhigh`→`high`, which is wrong for 4.6) and is not driven by model metadata. Also: grok-4.6 **cannot disable thinking** (`reasoning: {effort: none}` / `thinking.disabled` unsupported), yet the picker offers an Off toggle. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure Hermes with an xAI OAuth account, select `grok-4.6`. 2. Set reasoning effort to `high` in the desktop model menu. 3. Inspect the outgoing request body: no `reasoning.effort` field at all (allowlist miss → silently dropped). Expected: `reasoning: {effort: "high"}`. 4. Set effort to `max` or `ultra` (e.g. a pre-existing saved value): request fails with `400 {"error": "Invalid reasoning effort"}` — the entire turn is lost. ## Expected Behavior - Every model auto-reports its **real** supported effort levels (from models.dev `reasoning_options`), the picker shows exactly those, and the send path **clamps** any stored value to the nearest supported level — no silent drops, no 400s. - Models whose `reasoning_options` include a `toggle` (e.g. DeepSeek) get the Off switch; models like grok-4.6 that cannot turn thinking off do not. ## Actual Behavior - `grok_supports_reasoning_effort` allowlist in `agent/model_metadata.py` predates grok-4.6 → effort silently dropped. - `agent/transports/codex.py` hard-codes an outdated xAI effort map (folds `xhigh`→`high`; no catalog-driven clamp) → `max`/`ultra` reach the wire and 400. - Picker always renders the full 7-level Hermes scale (`minimal…ultra`) + Off toggle, regardless of the model (this half is being addressed by #85246). ## Live-Verified Effort Matrix (grok-4.6, api.x.ai /v1/responses) | effort | result | |---|---| | minimal / low / medium / high / xhigh | accepted | | max / ultra | **400 Invalid reasoning effort** | | none / thinking.disabled | unsupported — model still reasons | ## Root Cause `agent/model_metadata.py` `grok_supports_reasoning_effort()`: hard-coded model-name allowlist, not updated for grok-4.6. `agent/transports/codex.py`: effort handling has a static xAI-only map; no shared "allowed efforts for this model" concept. Both stem from discarding models.dev `reasoning_options` after parsing only the `reasoning` bool — the exact level list is available in the catalog and thrown away. ## Proposed Fix Data-driven, no hand-maintained allowlist: 1. `agent/models_dev.py`: parse `reasoning_options` into `ModelCapabilities.reasoning_efforts` (filtered to Hermes' scale) + `thinking_off` (has `toggle` / `none`). 2. `hermes_cli/inventory.py` `_apply_capabilities`: carry `reasoning_efforts` / `thinking_off` into the model-options payload (picker side, complements #85246). 3. `agent/models_dev.py` `clamp_reasoning_effort(effort, allowed)`: nearest-neighbor clamp for the send path; unknown models fall back to the full Hermes scale (current behavior). 4. `agent/transports/codex.py`: clamp the wire value to the model's catalog efforts before sending; drop the stale hard-coded xAI map. 5. Desktop picker renders only `reasoning_efforts`, and hides the Off toggle when `thinking_off=false` (complements #85246). Local implementation exists and passes: pytest 108/108 (incl. new `tests/agent/test_reasoning_options.py`), vitest 11/11, `tsc --noEmit` clean. ## Related - #85246 (picker-side filtering — complements this) - #85683 (xAI picker refresh / pin grok-4.6) - #85153 (reasoning_effort: none mishandled for non-reasoning models — same family)

signal.title: Prefer more official features as plugins to keep Hermes core minimal
signal.text: ## Summary Hermes already shows a strong direction I like: the core stays compact, while platform adapters, business flows, UI panes, and complex skills move into plugins. I would like the team to push this further so the default experience stays simple, and extra capabilities are explicitly opt-in. ## Why - A minimal core is easier to maintain, audit, and run. - Pluginized features can ship, roll back, and evolve independently. - Users can compose only the surfaces they actually need. ## Requested direction 1. Prefer pluginizing platform adapters, message-driven business modes, heavy UI surfaces, and expensive skills. 2. Keep core focused on runtime, sessions, memory, tool protocol, and security boundaries. 3. Make plugin discoverability and enablement clearer in docs and Desktop. ## Examples I like - Hermes-Bot-Mode as a Desktop plugin instead of a core UI change - Telegram Business Mode as an opt-in plugin - Separate plugin/skill/tool packages for heavy integrations ## Impact - Simpler default install - Lower maintenance surface in core - More modular user experience - Clearer upgrade path for optional capabilities

signal.title: copilot-acp: fallback providers not triggered when Copilot monthly quota is exhausted
signal.text: ## Description When using `copilot-acp` as the primary provider with `fallback_providers` configured, the fallback chain does **not** activate when GitHub Copilot returns a monthly quota exhaustion error. Instead of falling back to the next provider, the error is surfaced directly to the user. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure `copilot-acp` as primary provider: ```yaml model: provider: copilot-acp default: auto base_url: acp://copilot api_mode: chat_completions ``` 2. Configure fallback providers: ```yaml fallback_providers: - provider: opencode-zen model: big-pickle base_url: https://opencode.ai/zen/v1 api_mode: chat_completions - provider: openrouter model: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash base_url: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 api_mode: chat_completions - provider: openai-codex model: gpt-5.4-mini base_url: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex ``` 3. Have valid API keys for fallback providers (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENCODE_ZEN_API_KEY`). 4. Exhaust Copilot's monthly quota. 5. Send a message via Telegram or CLI — the agent returns the raw error instead of falling back. ## Error Message ``` Error: You have exceeded your monthly quota (Request ID: A540:22A007:3849658:44F52D9:6A541F53) ``` ## Analysis The Copilot ACP client (`agent/copilot_acp_client.py`) raises a `RuntimeError` when the subprocess exits early. The error message contains the word `"quota"` which exists in `_USAGE_LIMIT_PATTERNS` in `agent/error_classifier.py`, which should classify it as `FailoverReason.billing` with `should_fallback=True`. However, in practice the fallback chain is never activated. There appear to be two potential issues: 1. **Missing billing pattern**: `_BILLING_PATTERNS` has `"exceeded your current quota"` but the Copilot message says `"exceeded your *monthly* quota"` — the substring `"exceeded your current quota"` does not match `"exceeded your monthly quota"`. While `_USAGE_LIMIT_PATTERNS` does contain `"quota"`, the matching logic may not be reaching that check for ACP RuntimeErrors. 2. **ACP error path**: The RuntimeError from the ACP subprocess may be caught at a different level before reaching `classify_api_error()` in the conversation loop, bypassing the classification entirely. ## Environment - Hermes Agent (latest) - Provider: `copilot-acp` - Platform: Telegram gateway (also reproducible via CLI) - API keys for fallback providers are configured and valid ## Expected Behavior When Copilot ACP returns a quota exhaustion error, the fallback chain should activate and switch to the next configured provider (opencode-zen, then openrouter, etc.). ## Actual Behavior The error is surfaced directly without attempting fallback providers.

signal.title: ACP adapter: turns ending in text_response are silently dropped on Buzz-connected sessions (never published to relay)
signal.text: # ACP adapter: turns ending in `text_response` are silently dropped on Buzz-connected sessions (never published to relay) ## Summary On a Buzz-connected ACP persona ("Leo", running as a systemd-managed `buzz-acp-leo.service`), a conversation turn that ended with `reason=text_response` (i.e. the model's final output was plain assistant text with no accompanying tool call) was silently lost — never published to the Nostr relay, never retried, and never logged as an error. The user received no reply for 47 minutes and the ~1897-character status update is permanently unrecoverable. Turns that end via an explicit tool call (e.g. a "send to Buzz" action) are delivered correctly and logged as such, which strongly suggests the ACP↔Buzz bridge only treats tool-call-driven sends as requiring an explicit relay-publish step, and silently drops bare `text_response` turns. ## Environment - Hermes Agent, ACP adapter mode (`buzz-acp` persona integration) - Persona: "Leo", running as systemd service `buzz-acp-leo.service` on a self-hosted Hetzner box - Transport: Buzz relay (self-hosted), Nostr protocol backend for message publish/subscribe - Observed: 2026-08-12, via `journalctl -u buzz-acp-leo.service` ## Steps to Reproduce / Conditions Observed Not yet reproduced on demand — this is a single confirmed incident reconstructed from production logs. Condensed timeline (all UTC, 2026-08-12): 1. **01:45:26** — Leo sends a DM committing to two tracks of work ("On it. Splitting into two tracks: ..."). 2. **01:46:44** — New conversation turn begins, session `20260812_014644_fc0f12`, executing track 1. 3. **01:52:13** — Track 1 completes successfully: a review request is sent via an explicit tool call to a ticket-lane channel (confirmed via tool-call log line, event `fcbdf2cc...`). **This confirms the normal send path works when a turn ends via an explicit tool call.** 4. **01:55:57** — API call #13 completes (in=134509, out=676 tokens, latency=11.2s, cache=99%). Immediately followed by: `Turn ended: reason=text_response(finish_reason=stop) ... response_len=1897 session=20260812_014644_fc0f12` — the agent composed a ~1897-character status update as plain text, with **no tool call**. 5. **01:55:57 → 01:56:28** (31s, relay connection healthy) — **no publish/send/outbound log line appears anywhere** for this response. Delivery was never even attempted. 6. **01:56:28 → 02:20:39** — Unrelated relay websocket disconnect ("no pong received within 10s — connection dead, reconnecting"), ~24 min outage. Confirmed **coincidental, not causal** — the response vanished 31s *before* this outage began, while the connection was still up. 7. **02:20:39** — Relay reconnects and resubscribes to channels. No queue-flush, resend, or retry of the missing message occurs in the following 15+ minutes. 8. **Ground truth check** — Direct fetch of the DM channel from the relay shows nothing from Leo between 01:45:26 and 02:32:59 (47 minutes of silence). Human (Nick) pinged at 01:50:42 ("I don't understand. Are you working or not?") with no reply logged. Only after a second nag at 02:32:33 did Leo produce a **new, differently-worded** reply — not a delayed delivery of the original. The original 1897-char update is permanently lost with no trace, no error, no retry. ## Expected vs Actual Behavior **Expected:** Any final assistant response intended for the user — regardless of whether the turn ends via a tool call or via plain `text_response` — is published to the Buzz/Nostr relay, or a delivery failure is logged/retried/alerted. **Actual:** Turns ending in `reason=text_response` with no tool call appear to close without any publish attempt to the relay. No error, warning, or retry is logged. The message is silently and permanently dropped. ## Root Cause Analysis **Caveat: this is evidence-based inference from log analysis, not a traced code path.** We have not stepped through the actual ACP adapter / Buzz bridge source to confirm the exact mechanism — treat the following as a strong hypothesis, not a confirmed diagnosis. The pattern observed is consistent with the ACP↔Buzz bridge only wiring an explicit "publish to relay" action to tool-call-based sends (e.g. a `send_to_buzz`-style tool), while turns that end purely on `text_response` (plain final assistant text, `finish_reason=stop`, no tool call) are not recognized by the bridge as requiring an outbound publish at all. No error is raised because — from the adapter's perspective — nothing went wrong; it simply never routed that text anywhere. Likely candidate code areas (unverified, offered as starting points for investigation): - `acp_adapter/server.py` — turn completion / response handling - `buzz_acp` Rust relay client — outbound publish invocation sites - `agent/turn_finalizer.py` (or equivalent) — specifically the `text_response` finish-reason branch ## Related Issues This matches a broader known bug class already partially tracked upstream — same failure symptom (final assistant response generated but never delivered), different transport in each case: - **#10748** — "streaming mode silently drops final response when `already_sent` is true" (response stored in DB, never delivered). Same failure class; different transport (streaming path, not ACP/Buzz). - **#31884** — Telegram gateway can silently drop a turn with `response=0 chars` while internal work continues. Same failure class; Telegram gateway, not ACP/Buzz. - **#31588** — Messages sent while agent is busy get silently queued with no feedback. Related failure mode (silent loss of user-facing signal) but different trigger condition. Filing this as a **new issue** rather than a comment on #10748 because the transport and adapter code involved (ACP adapter, Buzz relay client, `text_response` turn-finalization path) is distinct from whatever code #10748/#31884/#31588 cover — but cross-linking all three here since they may share a root cause or fix pattern (i.e. "final response delivery must not depend on which finish_reason ended the turn"). ## Suggested Fix (suggestions only — not implemented or tested) **(a) Route text_response through the same explicit publish mechanism as tool-call sends.** For ACP/Buzz-bound sessions, make the bare "turn ends in plain text" case invoke the same explicit publish/send call used by tool-call-based sends, so there is no code path where a text-ending turn can complete without an outbound relay event being attempted. **(b) Add a post-turn delivery integrity check.** If a Buzz-bound session's turn ends with `reason=text_response` and no corresponding outbound Nostr event is emitted within a short window (e.g. a few seconds), log an ERROR and either retry the publish or alert, rather than allowing the turn to close silently. Either approach (or both, as belt-and-suspenders) would have caught this incident — (a) prevents the drop, (b) would have at minimum surfaced it as a visible error instead of 47 minutes of silent user-facing failure. ## Reproduction Status **Not reproduced on demand.** This report is based entirely on `journalctl` log analysis of a live production instance (`buzz-acp-leo.service`) after the incident was noticed via user complaint ("I don't understand. Are you working or not?"). No isolated repro case has been constructed yet. Happy to assist with building one if adapter maintainers can point to the relevant turn-finalization code, or if there's a known way to force a turn to end in `finish_reason=stop` with no tool call in a Buzz-connected test session.

signal.title: Fix Azure Foundry Responses post-tool replay
signal.text: ## Summary This patch fixes Azure Foundry Responses post-tool replay under `codex_responses`. Current upstream main reaches the post-tool follow-up request, but the follow-up input includes `function_call`, `function_call_output`, and `reasoning` items together. Azure Foundry rejects that payload with HTTP 400 `invalid_payload`. This patch scopes the behavior to Azure Foundry Responses and suppresses reasoning replay on post-tool turns while preserving `function_call` and `function_call_output` continuity. ## Why The initial model request and tool schema shape are not the root cause. The failure happens after tool execution, when the Responses follow-up input is constructed. On current upstream main, the debug harness reports: ```text likely failing phase: post-tool follow-up input input type values: function_call,function_call_output,reasoning invalid_payload: The provided data does not match the expected schema ``` With this patch branch, the same Foundry Project endpoint + Responses API debug harness completes successfully. The patched post-tool follow-up input contains `function_call` and `function_call_output`, but no replayed `reasoning` item. ## Validation * `uv run --with pytest --with pytest-timeout --with-editable ./hermes-agent python -m pytest hermes-agent/tests/agent/transports/test_codex_transport.py -q` * 62 passed * Validated with a Foundry Project endpoint + Responses API debug harness: * health passed: yes * capabilities HTTP status: 200 * model HTTP status: 200 * model marker returned: yes * tool HTTP status: 200 * tool request passed: yes * Also validated in an Azure Container Apps Sandboxes integration harness using a patched Hermes image: * model-directed Hermes tool routing passed: yes * workspace marker independently verified: yes ## Scope This change is intended to be narrow: * Azure Foundry Responses behavior is detected through the configured provider or Foundry Project endpoint host. * Reasoning replay suppression is scoped to Azure Foundry post-tool turns. * `function_call` and `function_call_output` continuity is preserved. * Existing non-Azure Responses behavior is covered by tests. ## Notes No secrets, endpoints, deployment names, tenant IDs, subscription IDs, client IDs, request IDs, or credentials are included.
signal.author: AshuJoshi

signal.title: fix(azure-foundry): scope Responses reasoning suppression to post-tool turns
signal.text: ## Summary Salvage of #59981, rebuilt on current `main`. Same root cause and same fix direction as @AshuJoshi's original; the diagnosis there was correct and is preserved. This version resolves the three blockers found in review and keeps his tests plus five new ones. Azure Foundry's OpenAI-compatible Responses surface rejects the **post-tool follow-up** payload with HTTP 400 `invalid_payload` when a replayed encrypted `reasoning` item is sent alongside `function_call` / `function_call_output`. The initial function-call request and ordinary multi-turn continuity are both accepted, so the failure only appears after the first tool executes and the follow-up input is constructed. `ResponsesApiTransport.build_kwargs` now detects the Foundry endpoint and drops only the encrypted reasoning replay on that follow-up turn, leaving `function_call` / `function_call_output` continuity intact. ## What changed relative to #59981 **1. No `chat_completion_helpers.py` change at all.** `main` already forwards `provider` and `base_url` to the Responses transport (lines 1443 and 1447). The original PR re-added both, which auto-merged into invalid Python: ``` SyntaxError: keyword argument repeated: provider ``` That is why the PR showed as `CONFLICTING`. Dropping the hunk entirely removes the conflict and the syntax error together — the detection has everything it needs from the existing call site. **2. Host matching uses `utils.base_url_host_matches`, not a substring test.** `".services.ai.azure.com" in base_url` also matches URLs that merely *carry* the domain: | base_url | substring | this PR | |---|---|---| | `https://myres.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/p/openai/v1` | ✅ | ✅ | | `https://proxy.example.com/.services.ai.azure.com/v1` | ✅ ❌ | ❌ | | `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1?upstream=.services.ai.azure.com` | ✅ ❌ | ❌ | | `https://services.ai.azure.com.evil.example/v1` | ✅ ❌ | ❌ | Suppressing reasoning replay on an unrelated provider silently degrades its cross-turn coherence. `base_url_host_matches` exists for exactly this false-positive class, its docstring names it, and every sibling detector in this transport already uses it. **3. `_is_post_tool_replay` tests the trailing messages, not the whole history.** The original scanned the entire history for *any* assistant tool call plus *any* tool result, so it latched on permanently: ``` user → assistant(tool_calls) → tool → assistant("done") → user("explain recursion") ^ reasoning suppressed here, and on every later turn ``` That is the all-turns behavior the scoping was meant to avoid, reached one turn later. The rejected payload is specifically the turn *ending* on a tool result, so that is what is matched — including a trailing run of parallel tool results. ## Validation Verified with `scripts/run_tests.sh`, the repo's canonical per-file-isolation runner that matches CI: ``` scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/ tests/run_agent/ 532 files, 5595 tests passed, 0 failed, 21 skipped ``` `ruff check` clean on all three touched files. **27 tests** (@AshuJoshi's, plus new coverage for the two defects above): - post-tool suppression on Foundry; reasoning preserved on non-Azure Responses - detection by provider id and by endpoint host, independently - three non-Foundry host lookalikes (path, query, suffix) keep reasoning - non-tool Foundry follow-up keeps reasoning - user turn after a completed tool call keeps reasoning — sticky-history guard - parallel tool results still suppress - an explicit `replay_encrypted_reasoning=False` is never re-enabled - live `build_api_kwargs` path for the post-tool, non-tool, and post-tool-then-user-turn shapes Each new guard was confirmed to catch its defect by reverting to the unscoped host match and whole-history scan: the three lookalike cases and both sticky-history guards fail, and pass with the fix. ## Not verified here I have no Azure Foundry credentials, so I did not reproduce the original HTTP 400 or re-confirm the fix against a live endpoint. **This change is verified at the payload-construction layer only.** The live evidence — the Foundry Project + Responses API debug harness and the Azure Container Apps integration run — is @AshuJoshi's, from #59981. A live re-check by someone with a Foundry deployment before merge would be worth having. Closes #59981.

signal.title: fix(discord): preserve thread routing for progress edits
signal.text: ## Summary Fix Discord progress-message edits that target the parent channel even when the message was originally sent inside a thread. - Resolve Discord edit targets from `metadata.thread_id`, falling back to `chat_id` when thread metadata is absent. - Preserve thread routing for long-running heartbeat edits, stale streamed-finalize reconciliation, and plugin-transformed final edits. - Keep legacy platform adapters compatible by passing metadata only when their `edit_message()` signature supports it. ## Root cause Discord progress sends honor `metadata.thread_id`, but `DiscordAdapter.edit_message()` previously fetched the message from the parent `chat_id`. Discord therefore returned `10008 Unknown Message` / HTTP 404 for a message that existed in the thread. ## Tests - Reproduced RED for adapter, heartbeat, stale-finalize, and transformed-response paths. - Focused routing tests: 5/5 normal and 5/5 optimized. - Discord edit/overflow tests: 9/9 normal and 9/9 optimized. - Kanban notifier tests: 9/9 normal and 9/9 optimized. - `py_compile`: 6/6. - `git diff --check`: PASS. - Independent pre-commit review: PASS (B0/M0/m0). ## Scope Six files changed. No schema, database, daemon, retry-policy, or credential changes.

signal.title: fix(redaction): mask array-style query credentials
signal.text: ## Summary - recognize PHP/Rails-style array query keys at strict credential-redaction boundaries - mask both literal `access_token[]=...` and percent-encoded `access_token%5B%5D=...` forms while preserving the original key spelling - preserve similarly named public parameters such as `token_count[]` and `access_tokenized[]` - cover the shared redactor plus compaction-summary and pre-compression memory-context paths ## Why Strict URL redaction decodes parameter names before exact sensitive-name matching. Array-style keys decoded to `access_token[]`, so they missed the canonical `access_token` entry and their values remained visible in persisted compaction summaries and memory context sent for compression. This focused PR extracts the independently useful shared-redactor fix from #35601, following the suggestion in [this review comment](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/35601#issuecomment-5288097879). It does not change default navigation redaction behavior; the stricter handling remains opt-in through `redact_url_credentials=True`. ## Validation - `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/test_redact.py tests/agent/test_compaction_redaction_boundaries.py tests/agent/test_pre_compress_memory_context.py tests/agent/test_context_compressor.py tests/test_redaction_registry.py -q` - 268 passed - regression-proof run against the pre-fix implementation - 5 focused assertions failed, then passed with the fix restored - Ruff on all changed Python files - Python compilation and `git diff --check` Related to #35601.
